narrative:
The model estimated a 96.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and the law school admission decision followed that high-risk prediction. This does not mean the school concluded you cannot succeed; it means the application was denied because the model judged first-time bar failure very likely.

The strongest factor was your class standing in year three. You were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile, so this substantially increased the predicted risk. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor: a 26 compared with an accepted-student average of about 37 pushed the prediction toward failure. Your year-one class standing, also in the first decile, was the third most important factor and likewise increased the risk, though less than your later standing. Your undergraduate GPA was close to the accepted average, so it was not among the main reasons for denial.

To improve a future application, focus on the factors weighed most: retake the LSAT after structured preparation, seek academic support or additional coursework to strengthen your record, and ask an admissions advisor how to explain your class-standing context. Consider delaying reapplication until you can show clear improvement, and use bar-exam preparation resources to address the readiness concern directly.
